description_full: Academy Sports and Outdoors, Inc., through its subsidiaries, operates as a sporting goods and outdoor recreational retailer in the United States. The company's outdoors division comprises camping products, such as coolers and drinkware, camping accessories and equipment, and watersports and equipment; fishing products, including marine equipment and fishing rods, reels, and baits and equipment; and hunting products, which includes firearms, ammunition, archery and archery equipment, camouflage apparel, waders, shooting accessories, gun safes, optics, airguns, and hunting equipment. Its sports and recreation division offers fitness equipment, fitness accessories, and nutrition supplies; team and specialty sports equipment, including baseball, football, basketball, soccer, golf, racket sports, volleyball, backpacks, and sports bags; recreation products, which includes patio furniture, outdoor cooking, trampolines, and play sets, as well as wheeled goods that include bicycles, skateboards, and other ride-on toys; and electronics, watches, and sunglasses, as well as front-end products, such as consumables, batteries, etc. The company's apparel division provides outdoor and seasonal apparel, denim, work apparel, graphic t-shirts, accessories, and outerwear; boys and girls outdoor, and athletic apparel and swimwear; sporting and fitness apparel; and professional and collegiate team licensed apparel and accessories. Its footwear division offers casual shoes, slippers, seasonal footwear, and socks; work and western boots, shoes, and hunting footwear; boys and girls footwear; athletic footwear, such as running shoes, athletic lifestyle, and training shoes; and team and specialty sports footwear, and slides. The company sells its products under the Academy Sports + Outdoors, Magellan Outdoors, BCG, O'rageous, Game Winner, Outdoor Gourmet, Freely, R.O.W., Redfield, and H2OX brand names. Academy Sports and Outdoors, Inc. was founded in 1938 and is headquartered in Katy, Texas.

financial_summary: Academy Sports and Outdoors, In is a mid-cap consumer cyclical business with a $4.2B market cap on $6.1B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at -2% over the past three years — essentially flat, and a business treading water is rarely a path to compounding.
Returns on capital run at 27% against a 10% cost of capital — a 17-point spread that is the clearest signature of an economic moat, with gross margins sitting at 34%.

The business throws off $222M in free cash flow — roughly 4 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 1.15× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, leverage is comfortably conservative at 0.2× net debt/EBITDA, and interest coverage of 15× is fortress-like.

Management returns a meaningful 5.6% of market cap to owners through dividends and buybacks, a strong signal of disciplined capital allocation, and insider ownership is negligible, so management has little personal stake in the long-term outcome.

sect: Its 8% operating margin is roughly in line with the Consumer Cyclical median (7%).
Its share of sector profits slightly exceeds its share of revenue (1.07x).

Over five years it has been losing share of the sector profit pool (-10.3% a year).
The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.03 across 377 companies in the universe; the top four hold 26% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares are in a strong uptrend, up 24% over the past year excluding the latest month.
The price sits near the top of its 52-week range, 5% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 45% and a beta of 1.14, it moves roughly with the market, though its beta has shifted (1y 0.15 vs 5y 1.22), so read it loosely.
About $80.3M trades a day, enough to build a position.
In past sell-offs it fell 37% in the 2022 bear market.
val: The stock trades only 11% below its DCF fair value of $75.82, a thin margin of safety.
The fair-value models disagree (dispersion 48%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $56.15 to $104 (P10-P90), so treat the estimate as noisy.
On multiples it looks cheap against Consumer Cyclical peers: P/E 11.3 vs 18.8 and EV/EBITDA 8.3 vs 10.7 (sector median).
Against its own history it is dear: the EBIT multiple sits 68% above its 10-year median.
Earnings yields are attractive: an FCF yield of 5.3% (above the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 8.8% (vs the 8% bar).
The 19 covering analysts target $62.37 on average, 8% below the price.
prof: ROIC of 27% clears the cost of capital of 9.7% by 17pp, the mark of a value creator; returns have swung a lot from year to year (CV 0.37).
It runs a 34% gross margin and converts 4% of revenue into free cash flow.
Earnings quality looks solid: a Piotroski score of 7/9 and cash conversion of 1.15x.
ROE of 17% comes mostly from margins and asset turnover rather than leverage (2.4x equity multiplier).
It spends 0.3% of revenue on stock compensation.
hlth: Leverage is conservative at 0.2x net debt to EBITDA ($330.3M of cash against $483.8M of debt), with interest covered 14.6x.
growth: Revenue has compounded at -1.8% over 3 years and 1.2% over 5 years, so growth is decelerating.
At current returns, reinvesting 66% of profits supports about 17.7% a year of fundamental growth, enough to sustain growth.
Free cash flow has compounded -25.5% a year over five years, short of the 5% durability bar.
Capex runs 1.7x depreciation (3.5% of sales), so it is building capacity for future growth.
Its Rule of 40 score is 5, below the 40 that marks a healthy growth business.
own: Insiders own a modest 1.6%, and reported institutional holdings exceed 100% of shares (a sign of heavy share lending).
Insiders have only sold over the past year (8 sales, net $5.9M sold).
It returns 5.6% a year to shareholders (4.8% in buybacks and 0.9% in dividends).
The share count has shrunk 6.8% a year over five years, steadily raising each holder's stake.
Short interest is elevated at 19.9% of the float, 5.8 days to cover.
people: With about 22,000 employees, each generates about $275K of revenue, 0.7x the Consumer Cyclical median.
That works out to $10K of free cash flow per employee.
CEO pay is $2.6M (9x revenue per employee), and compensation governance scores well (3/10, lower is better).
